what_its_for: Etanercept is used to treat conditions where your immune system attacks your own body. These include rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis (spine arthritis), plaque psoriasis (a skin condition), and juvenile idiopathic arthritis in children. It works by blocking a protein in your body called TNF that causes inflammation and pain.
how_to_take: Etanercept is given as an injection under the skin (subcutaneous injection). It comes as a prefilled syringe, an autoinjector pen, or a powder you mix with liquid. Common injection sites include the front of your thighs, your belly (at least 2 inches away from your belly button), or the outer area of your upper arms. Rotate your injection site each time — do not inject into the same spot twice in a row. Do not inject into skin that is red, bruised, tender, hard, or scarred. Let the medication warm up to room temperature for about 15 to 30 minutes before injecting — do not microwave it. Clean the injection site with an alcohol swab and let it dry before injecting. Your doctor or nurse will teach you how to inject yourself properly before you do it on your own.
dosing: The dose depends on your condition, weight, and age. For most adults with rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or ankylosing spondylitis, the usual dose is 50 mg once a week OR 25 mg twice a week given 3 to 4 days apart. For adult plaque psoriasis, the starting dose may be 50 mg twice a week for 3 months, then reduced to 50 mg once a week. For children, the dose is based on body weight and is determined by your child's doctor. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, inject it as soon as you remember. However, if your next scheduled dose is very soon, skip the missed dose and get back on your regular schedule. Do not inject two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your doctor or pharmacist.
storage: Store etanercept in the refrigerator at 36°F to 46°F (2°C to 8°C). Do NOT freeze it — if it has been frozen, throw it away and get a new dose. Keep it in its original carton to protect it from light. If needed, you may store it at room temperature (up to 77°F or 25°C) for up to 14 days, but once removed from the refrigerator do not put it back. Throw it away if not used within those 14 days. Keep out of reach of children. Do not shake the medication. Dispose of used syringes and needles in a puncture-resistant sharps container — never throw loose needles in the trash.
what_to_avoid: Do not receive live vaccines while taking etanercept — these include vaccines like MMR (measles, mumps, rubella), varicella (chickenpox), nasal flu spray, yellow fever, and shingles (Zostavax). Ask your doctor about safe vaccines before starting treatment. Avoid close contact with people who are sick, as etanercept lowers your ability to fight infections. Avoid excessive sun exposure and tanning beds if you have psoriasis, and always use sunscreen. Do not start etanercept if you currently have any active infection, including skin infections or open sores. Limit alcohol use. Do not use etanercept with certain other biologics like abatacept (Orencia) or anakinra (Kineret) without your doctor's guidance, as this can increase infection risk.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or seek emergency care if you notice: signs of a serious infection such as fever, chills, cough, shortness of breath, painful urination, or a wound that will not heal; signs of an allergic reaction such as hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; signs of heart failure such as swelling in your legs or feet, sudden weight gain, or shortness of breath; new or worsening numbness, tingling, vision problems, weakness, or dizziness (possible nervous system issues); unusual bruising or bleeding; extreme fatigue or pale skin; any new skin changes or sores; or if you think you may have been exposed to tuberculosis (TB). Also tell your doctor before any surgery or dental procedure.
when_it_works: Etanercept does not work overnight. Most people begin to notice some improvement in symptoms like joint pain, swelling, and stiffness within 2 to 4 weeks of starting treatment. Full benefits for arthritis may take up to 3 to 6 months. For psoriasis, you may see skin improvement within a few weeks, with the best results usually seen around 3 months. It is important to keep using it even if you feel well — stopping treatment may cause your symptoms to come back.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Talk to your doctor before using etanercept if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. It may affect your baby's immune system if used in the third trimester. Children: Etanercept is approved for children 2 years and older for juvenile idiopathic arthritis and 4 years and older for plaque psoriasis. Doses are weight-based. Older adults: Older adults may have a higher risk of infections while using this medication — report any signs of infection to your doctor promptly. Patients with diabetes: Monitor blood sugar closely, as some patients have noticed changes in blood sugar levels. Patients with a history of tuberculosis (TB) or hepatitis B: You will need special testing before starting etanercept, as it can reactivate these infections.
